'''Castle Fraser''' is a large [[Z-plan castle]] near [[Kemnay, Aberdeenshire|Kemnay]], [[Aberdeenshire]], Scotland. It is considered one of the most elaborate examples of its type and one of the grandest of the 'Castles of Mar'. The castle stands in over {{convert|300|acre|km2}} of landscaped grounds, woodland and farmland, including a 19th-century walled kitchen garden. There is [[Archaeology|archaeological]] evidence of an older square tower dating from around 1400 or 1500 within the current construction. The castle is a Category A [[listed building]]<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=LB2924|desc=Castle Fraser|access-date=18 June 2020}}</ref> and the grounds are included in the [[Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes in Scotland]].<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=GDL00091|desc=Castle Fraser|access-date=18 June 2020|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

== Construction ==
Originally known as ''Muchall-in-Mar'', construction of the elaborate, five-storey [[Z-plan castle]] was begun in 1575 by the 6th Laird of Fraser, Michael Fraser, on the basis of an earlier tower, and was completed in 1636. A panel on the northern side of the castle is signed ''"I Bel"'', believed to be the [[Mason's mark|mark]] of the master mason John Bell of Midmar. The castle is a joint creation over several decades with another master mason of this period, Thomas Leiper.<ref>{{cite web |title=Castle Fraser |url=http://canmore.rcahms.gov.uk/en/site/18722/details/castle+fraser/ |website=Canmore |publisher=Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Scotland |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120813231523/http://canmore.rcahms.gov.uk/en/site/18722/details/castle+fraser/ |archive-date=13 August 2012 |access-date=23 March 2026}}</ref>

Castle Fraser is contemporary with other nearby castles: [[Craigievar Castle]], [[Crathes Castle]] and [[Midmar Castle]] which are also believed to have been designed by the Bell family of master masons.

The castle was modernised in a classical style in the late 18th century, with a new entrance inserted in the south side and sash windows throughout. This work was supervised by [[Elyza Fraser]], the lady laird, assisted by [[Mary Bristow]]. Elyza was also responsible for the landscaping of the grounds, sweeping away the remains of the original formal gardens and orchards, and for the construction of the impressive octagonal stable block.

The interiors of the building were entirely reconstructed again between 1820 and 1850, by Charles Fraser, using the architects [[John Smith (architect)|John Smith]] and William Burn. The Library is a fine example of John Smith's regency style with Tudor detailing. Many of William Burn's more extravagant Gothic designs for the most important rooms were not carried out, although a Gothic-style pipe organ was installed (now removed to St Anne’s Scottish Episcopal Church in Kemnay).

External works during this period included the construction of the twin gatehouses (still extant), and a grand domed stair and access corridors with loggias in the courtyard (removed). The castle was partially restored by the new owners around 1950. The architect and antiquary Dr William Kelly supervised the removal of much 19th-century work to reveal the earlier fabric.

Castle Fraser retains the atmosphere of a family home and still contains the original contents, including Fraser family portraits, furniture and collections. The evocative interiors represent all periods of the castle's history, from the Medieval stone vaulted Great Hall to the Regency Dining Room.

== Ownership ==
Castle Fraser was built as the home of the Frasers of Muchalls, later Frasers of Castle Fraser. The castle was passed down through the Lords Fraser, the Frasers of Inverallochy and then the Mackenzie family who took the name Mackenzie Fraser. In 1897 the last male Fraser of the direct line, Frederick Mackenzie Fraser, died childless. In 1921 his widow, Theodora, sold the castle due to the lack of a suitable heir and mounting financial difficulties.  The buyer was [[Weetman Pearson, 1st Viscount Cowdray]], who gave it to his son, [[Bernard Clive Pearson]] for restoration. The castle then passed onto Lavinia Pearson and her husband Major Charles Michael Smiley. The Pearson family then gave the castle to the [[National Trust for Scotland]] in 1976.<ref>{{cite web |title=Scottish Castles Photo Library - Castle Fraser, Aberdeenshire |url=http://www.rampantscotland.com/castles/blcastles_fraser.htm |website=Rampant Scotland |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260213084546/http://www.rampantscotland.com/castles/blcastles_fraser.htm |archive-date=13 February 2026 |access-date=23 March 2026}}</ref> The Trust now opens the castle to visitors all year round along with the grounds and walled garden. During 2019, the site received 56,822 visitors.<ref name="ALVA 2019 visitor numbers">{{cite web |title=ALVA - Association of Leading Visitor Attractions |url=https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 |website=www.alva.org.uk |access-date=18 November 2020}}</ref>

Some scenes in the 2006 film ''[[The Queen (2006 film)|The Queen]]'', starring [[Helen Mirren|Dame Helen Mirren]], featured Castle Fraser as a backdrop.<ref>{{cite web|title=Castles of Scotland - Castle Fraser |url=http://www.britainirelandcastles.com/Scotland/Aberdeenshire/Castle-Fraser.html |publisher=britainirelandcastles.com |access-date=17 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140102192814/http://www.britainirelandcastles.com/Scotland/Aberdeenshire/Castle-Fraser.html |archive-date=2 January 2014 |url-status=live |df=dmy }}</ref>

626746.title: Drum Castle
626746.extract: Drum Castle is a castle near Drumoak in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. For centuries it was the seat of the chief of Clan Irvine.  The place-name Drum is derived from Gaelic druim, 'ridge'. The site is located approximately 6+1⁄2 miles (10.5 kilometres) northeast of Banchory and 3 miles (5 kilometres) west of Peterculter. The property is now owned by the National Trust for Scotland and is open to the public.

'''Drum Castle''' is a [[castle]] near [[Drumoak]] in [[Aberdeenshire]], Scotland. For centuries it was the seat of the chief of [[Clan Irvine]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/drum-castle |title=Drum Castle |publisher=The National Trust for Scotland |access-date=7 November 2018 |archive-date=7 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181107145147/https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/drum-castle |url-status=live }}</ref>  The place-name Drum is derived from [[Scottish Gaelic|Gaelic]] ''druim'', 'ridge'.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.irvinehistory.com/Drum_Castle/Drum_Castle.htm |title=Drum Castle |access-date=26 January 2020 |archive-date=8 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230208232152/http://irvinehistory.com/Drum_Castle/Drum_Castle.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> The site is located approximately {{convert|6+1/2|mi|km|abbr=off|round=0.5}} northeast of Banchory and {{convert|3|mi|km|0|abbr=off}} west of Peterculter. The property is now owned by the [[National Trust for Scotland]] and is open to the public.

==History==
The original 13th-century tower of Drum Castle has been suggested as the work of [[medieval]] architect [[Richard Cementarius]], who built the [[Brig o' Balgownie]], the first Bridge of Don, in [[Old Aberdeen]].  It is believed to be one of the three oldest [[tower house]]s in Scotland (and notably unaltered). 

The castle and its grounds were granted to William de Irwyn in 1323 by [[Robert the Bruce]], and remained in the possession of [[Clan Irvine]] until 1975. William de Irwyn (of the Irvings of Bonshaw clan) was armour bearer/secretary (and neighbour) to King Robert the Bruce.

When [[Mary, Queen of Scots]], was [[progresses of Mary, Queen of Scots|travelling near Aberdeen]] in August 1564 she sent a messenger to the Laird of Drum asking him to make provisions for her, and may have visited the castle.<ref>Michael Pearce, "Account of George Wishart of Drymme", ''Miscellany of the Scottish History Society'', 17 (Edinburgh: SHS, 2025), p. 31.</ref> A large wing was added in 1619 by the 9th [[laird]] of Drum, and further alterations were made during the [[Victorian era]]. In June 1636, Sir Alexander Irvine of Drum and his wife Magdalene Scrimgeour were censured for harbouring the outlaw [[Gilderoy (Outlaw)|Gilderoy]].<ref>William Fraser, ''The Chiefs of Grant'', vol. 3 (Edinburgh, 1883), pp. 62–3.</ref> Drum played a role in the [[Covenanter|Covenanting Rebellion]] (as did nearby [[Muchalls Castle]]) leading to its being attacked and sacked three times.

[[File:MA(1829) p.210 - Drum - John Preston Neale.jpg|thumb|The castle in 1829 (by John Preston Neale)]]

In the 19th century, it was the home of [[Alexander Forbes Irvine]] of Drum. He had inherited the estate in 1861, on the death of his father. In 1875/1876, he arranged for a restoration of the courtyard, and the addition of an arched entrance and angle tower.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.irvinehistory.com/Drum_Castle/Drum_Castle.htm |title=Drum Castle |access-date=26 January 2020 |archive-date=8 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230208232152/http://irvinehistory.com/Drum_Castle/Drum_Castle.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[https://britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/200334097-drum-castle-drumoak#.Xi3noWhKhPY Drum Castle]</ref> He was also partly responsible for a restoration of the chapel.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.scottishchurches.org.uk/sites/site/id/478/name/Drum+Castle+Chapel+Drumoak+Grampian |title=Drum Castle Chapel |access-date=26 January 2020 |archive-date=26 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200126192936/http://www.scottishchurches.org.uk/sites/site/id/478/name/Drum%2BCastle%2BChapel%2BDrumoak%2BGrampian |url-status=dead }}</ref>

There was an older church located here; it was modified to create the chapel in the 1500s and 1600s. In 1857, the west window was enlarged and the cross was added; a new roof was also installed and some restoration of the interior was completed.<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=LB3114|desc=Drum Castle, Chapel}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://scottishchurches.org.uk/sites/site/id/478/name/Drum+Castle+Chapel+Drumoak+Grampian |title=Drum Castle Chapel |access-date=26 January 2020 |archive-date=26 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200126192936/http://www.scottishchurches.org.uk/sites/site/id/478/name/Drum%2BCastle%2BChapel%2BDrumoak%2BGrampian |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The site was once served by [[Drum railway station]] on the [[Deeside Railway]]. Service was discontinued in 1951.

==Recent status==
The castle has been a Category-A Listed property since 1987. The report states that the agreement with the National Trust was made in 1964 by Mr H.Q. Forbes Irvine, the 24th Laird, and that the agreement came into force in 1976, after 650 years of ownership by the Irvine Lairds. The summary states that the tower was built in 1280–1300, that the Jacobean Wing was added in 1619 and that modifications were made ca. 1800, 1840 and 1875. The Chapel is Category-B Listed as are the Walled Garden and East Lodge; in 1987, the garden was "derelict".<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=GDL00141|desc=Drum Castle|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

The [[chapel]], dining hall and estate may be hired for weddings and corporate functions. The current (early 2020) NTS website, however, discusses its Garden of Historic Roses, spread out over four distinct areas. The grand Victorian library with over 4,000 books was one of the attractions; the castle was also offering a "programme of temporary exhibitions throughout the year".<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/drum-castle |title=Drum Castle |access-date=7 November 2018 |archive-date=7 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181107145147/https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/drum-castle |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>[https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/drum-castle/highlights/castle Drum Castle Highlights]</ref> A tourism website added that the castle "contains superb furniture and paintings. In the 16th-century chapel are a beautiful stained glass window and the Augsburg silver Madonna". The site has a playground, a small shop and a tearoom.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Drum Castle Garden (NTS) - Gardens - Aberdeen, Aberdeenshire and Moray - by Banchory |url=https://www.daysoutscotland.com/aberdeen-aberdeenshire-and-moray/gardens/listing/drum-castle-garden-nts |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200126191647/https://www.daysoutscotland.com/aberdeen-aberdeenshire-and-moray/gardens/listing/drum-castle-garden-nts |archive-date=2020-01-26 |access-date=2025-12-06 |website=Days Out Scotland |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The castle, gardens and estate are open to visitors throughout the year.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://whichmuseum.com/scotland/drumoak/drum-castle-garden-and-estate |title=Drum Castle, Garden and Estate |access-date=26 January 2020 |archive-date=26 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200126192436/https://whichmuseum.com/scotland/drumoak/drum-castle-garden-and-estate |url-status=live }}</ref> During 2019, 47,446 people visited the castle.<ref name="ALVA 2019 visitor numbers">{{cite web |title=ALVA – Association of Leading Visitor Attractions |url=https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 |website=www.alva.org.uk |access-date=18 November 2020 |archive-date=7 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120307140834/https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Area's ancient history==
Prehistoric habitation of the local area is known through archaeological sites such as [[Balbridie]]. [[Roman legion]]s marched from [[Raedykes]] to nearby [[Normandykes]] as they sought higher ground evading the [[bog]]s of [[Red Moss, Aberdeenshire|Red Moss]] and other low-lying mosses associated with the [[Burn of Muchalls]]. That march used the [[Elsick Mounth]], one of the ancient [[trackway]]s crossing the [[Grampian Mountains]]; the situation of the Elsick Mounth terminating at a ford to the River Dee is thought to have been instrumental in the strategic siting of Drum Castle as a point to monitor traffic on the Elsick Mounth<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=18037|title=Elsick Mounth|website=The Megalithic Portal}}</ref> lying west of [[Netherley, Scotland|Netherley]].

This harled castle was built by the Burnetts of Leys and was owned by the family for almost 400 years. The castle and its grounds are currently owned and managed by the National Trust for Scotland and are open to the public.

'''Crathes Castle''' (pronounced {{IPAc-en|ˈ|k|r|æ|θ|ɪ|s}} {{respell|KRATH|iss}}) is a [[castle]] built in the 16th century, near [[Banchory]] in [[Aberdeenshire]], [[Scotland]]. It is in the historic county of [[Kincardineshire]]. This [[harl]]ed castle was built by the Burnetts of Leys and was owned by the family for almost 400 years. The castle and its grounds are currently owned and managed by the [[National Trust for Scotland]] and are open to the public.

==History==
Crathes sits on land given as a gift to the [[House of Burnett|Burnetts of Ley family]] by King [[Robert the Bruce]] in 1323.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jervise |first=Andrew |title=Memorials of Angus and the Mearns : being an account, historical, antiquarian, and traditionary of the castles and towns visited by Edward I, and of the barons, clergy, and others, who swore fealty to England in 1291-6 ; also, of the Abbey of Cupar, and the Priory of Rostinoth, to which is added an appendix of original documents |publisher=Adam & Charles Black |year=1861 |edition=1 |location=Edinburgh |pages=19}}</ref>

In the 14th and 15th centuries, the Burnett of Leys built a fortress of timbers on an island they made in the middle of a nearby bog. This method of fortification, known as a [[crannog]], was common in the [[Late Middle Ages]]. Construction of the current tower house of Crathes Castle was begun in 1553<ref name="GommeMaguire2008">{{cite book|last1=Gomme|first1=Andor|last2=Maguire|first2=Alison|title=Design and Plan in the Country House: From Castle Donjons to Palladian Boxes|url={{GBurl|id=9QyzoRo_c0cC|pg=PA31}}|year=2008|publisher=Yale University Press|isbn=978-0-300-12645-7|page=31}}</ref> but delayed several times during its construction due to political problems during the reign of [[Mary, Queen of Scots]].

It was completed in 1596 by [[Alexander Burnett of Leys]], and an additional wing added in the 18th century. Alexander Burnett, who completed the construction of Crathes, began a new project, the early 17th-century reconstruction of nearby [[Muchalls Castle]]. That endeavour was completed by his son, [[Sir Thomas Burnett, 1st Baronet|Sir Thomas Burnett]].

In 1877, Sir Robert Burnett transformed the Great Hall by adding oak panelling and gilded leather in a faux-medieval style, to satisfy his New York wife Matilda and her guests that they were living in a truly old structure. Robert also purchased a whole new suite of furnishings for the entire structure of both antique and faux antique style as he thought befitted the house. Several painted beam ceilings, long covered by Georgian plasterwork, were re-exposed in 1913 during construction works (they had been spotted during the 1877 works and recovered).{{sfn|Gow|2008}}

Crathes Castle served as the ancestral seat of the [[Burnetts of Leys]] until [[Sir James Burnett, 13th Baronet]] gave it to the [[National Trust for Scotland]] in 1951.<ref name="Black2011">{{cite book|last=Black|first=Jonathan|title=The Face of Courage: Eric Kennington, Portraiture and the Second World War|url={{GBurl|id=UeoyygujmVwC|pg=PA144}}|date=15 July 2011|publisher=Philip Wilson Publishers|isbn=978-0-85667-705-2|page=144}}</ref> The family continued to live in the house.

The Great Hall was stripped back to its bare stone walls in 1953.{{sfn|Gow|2008}}{{Full citation needed|date=September 2023}}

Another historically important structure in this region linked to the Burnett of Leys family is [[Monboddo House]].

==Fire==
A fire damaged portions of the castle (in particular the [[Anne, Queen of Great Britain|Queen Anne]] wing) on 6 January 1966.

After the fire the laird, James Cecil Burnett was limited to the use of "a stump of the service wing" as his actual residence. The quarters and possessions of the on-site National Trust representative, Miss Jean Dodds, were wholly destroyed. It was decided by the National Trust's resident architect [[Schomberg Scott]] that the Queen Anne wing should be rebuilt to its original height of two storeys and that the Victorian wing should be wholly demolished.{{sfn|Gow|2008}}{{Full citation needed|date=September 2023}}

The insurance company paid £65,000; half of which was used to build the Burnetts a new house detached from the castle.{{sfn|Gow|2008}}{{Full citation needed|date=September 2023}}

==Interior==
The castle contains a significant collection of portraits, and intriguing original [[Scottish renaissance painted ceilings]] survive in several [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean]] rooms: the ''Chamber of the Muses'', the ''Chamber of Nine Worthies'' and the ''Green Lady's Room''.<ref name="ScotlandScotland1987">{{cite book|title=Scottish Renaissance interiors|url={{GBurl|id=7scLAQAAMAAJ}}|year=1987|publisher=Moubray House Press in association with the National Trust for Scotland and the Historic Houses Association for Scotland|page=19}}</ref>

[[Domestic furnishing in early modern Scotland|Original furniture still in the house]] and on display includes a carved bed and two [[caquetoire]] chairs dating from 1597 and bearing the owners' initials and heraldry.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Jackson|first=Stephen|title=The Scottish Caquetoire Chair|journal=Regional Furniture|volume=35|year=2021|pages=100–101}}</ref>

==Garden and grounds==
The castle estate is {{convert|240|ha|acre km2}} and contains {{convert|530|acre|ha acre km2|abbr=on|order=out}} of woodlands and fields, including nearly {{convert|4|acre|ha acre m2|round=0.5|abbr=on|order=out}} of [[walled garden]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britainirelandcastles.com/Scotland/Aberdeenshire/Crathes-Castle.html|title=Crathes Castle|publisher=Britainirelandcastles.com|accessdate=14 April 2014}}</ref> Within the walled garden are gravel paths with surrounding specimen plants, mostly in herbaceous borders. Many of the plants are labelled with taxonomic descriptions. There is also a grass croquet court at a higher terraced level within the walled garden. Ancient [[topiary]] hedges of Irish yew dating from 1702 separate the gardens into eight themed areas.<ref name="Goulty2003">{{cite book|last=Goulty|first=Sheena MacKellar|title=Heritage Gardens: Care, Conservation, Management|url={{GBurl|id=KEaIAgAAQBAJ|pg=PA23-IA1}}|date=2 September 2003|publisher=Routledge|isbn=1-134-90478-9|page=23}}</ref> Crathes and its grounds are open to tourists throughout the year. A visitor centre provides information about the castle and its surroundings. There is a tea shop on site and a car park for any size of car.

==Mesolithic calendar==
In 2004 excavations at the castle uncovered a series of pits believed to date from about 10,000 years ago. The find was analysed in 2013 and is considered to be the world's oldest known [[lunar calendar]] dating from 8000 BC to about 4000 BC.<ref name=Yahoo7>{{cite news|title='WORLD'S OLDEST CALENDAR' DISCOVERED IN SCOTTISH FIELD| url=http://au.news.yahoo.com/queensland/a/-/world/18007882/worlds-oldest-calendar-discovered-in-scottish-field/| accessdate=15 July 2013| newspaper=Yahoo7| date=15 July 2013}}</ref> This dating would make the structure up to five thousand years older<ref name=Yahoo7/> than previously recorded time-measuring monuments in [[Mesopotamia]].<ref name=BBC/>

The site of [[Warren Field]] was identified from aerial photography when unusual crop marks were seen by the [[Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Scotland]].<ref name=BBC>{{cite news| title='World's oldest calendar' discovered in Scottish field| url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-north-east-orkney-shetland-23286928| accessdate=15 July 2013| publisher=BBC| date=15 July 2013}}</ref>

626772.title: Craigievar Castle
626772.extract: Craigievar Castle is a harled castle or fortified country house 6 miles (9.7 km) south of Alford, Aberdeenshire, Scotland. It was the seat of Clan Sempill, and the Forbes family resided here for 350 years until 1963, when the property was sold to the National Trust for Scotland by the 19th Lord Sempill.

main.*:
{{short description|Castle in Aberdeenshire, Scotland}} {{Use dmy dates|date=January 2018}} {{Use British English|date=January 2018}} {{Infobox Castle | name = Craigievar Castle | image = Craigievar Doocot and Castle - geograph.org.uk - 7846018.jpg | image_size = 250px | caption = Craigievar Castle in 2024 | map_type = Scotland | website = {{URL|https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/craigievar|Craigievar Castle}} {{designation list | embed = yes | designation1 = Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes in Scotland | designation1_offname = Craigievar Castle | designation1_date = 1 July 1987 | designation1_number = {{Historic Environment Scotland|num=GDL00114|short=yes}} }} }} '''Craigievar Castle''' is a [[harl]]ed castle or fortified country house {{convert|6|mi}} south of [[Alford, Aberdeenshire|Alford]], [[Aberdeenshire]], Scotland. It was the seat of [[Clan Sempill]], and the Forbes family resided here for 350 years until 1963, when the property was sold to the [[National Trust for Scotland]] by [[William Forbes-Sempill, 19th Lord Sempill|the 19th Lord Sempill]].{{cite web |title=Craigievar Castle, a Scottish castle full of tales of warriors and ghosts|date=10 September 2020 |url=https://www.countrylife.co.uk/architecture/craigievar-castle-a-scottish-castle-full-of-tales-of-warriors-and-ghosts-218361 |publisher=Country Life |accessdate=16 September 2020}} ==History== An example of the original [[Scottish baronial style|Scottish Baronial]] architecture, the seven-storey castle was completed in 1626 by the [[Aberdeen|Aberdonian]] merchant [[William Forbes (merchant)|William Forbes]], ancestor of the [[Forbes baronets]] of Craigievar and brother of the [[Bishop of Aberdeen]], Patrick Forbes of [[Corse Castle]]. Forbes purchased the partially completed structure from the impoverished Mortimer family in the year 1610. He arranged for the continued construction, completing it in 1625 or 1626. Forbes was nicknamed "Danzig Willy", a reference to his shrewd international trading success with the [[Baltic states]].{{citation |title=The National Trust for Scotland guide |editor-last=Prentice |editor-first=Robin |year=1978 |isbn=0-224-01632-6|publisher=Cape |pages=59–60}} Some used the nickname "Willy the Merchant", also based on the substantial profits he made while "merchandising at Dantzick", according to one source. William's son became a [[baronet of Nova Scotia]] by [[Charles I of England|Charles I]]; this title is now extant. The Forbes Baronetcy, of Craigievar in the County of Aberdeen, was created in the Baronetage of Nova Scotia on 20 April 1630 for William Forbes. He was also a descendant of Hon. Patrick Forbes, third son of the second Lord Forbes, and the nephew of the first baronet of the 1628 creation. The fourth baronet represented [[Aberdeenshire (UK Parliament constituency)|Aberdeenshire]] in the [[British House of Commons|House of Commons]]. The 5th Baronet married the Hon. Sarah Sempill, eldest daughter of Hugh Sempill, 12th Lord Sempill. Their grandson, the eighth Baronet, succeeded as seventeenth Lord Sempill in 1884 (see the [[Lord Sempill]] for earlier history of this title). The titles remained united until the death of his grandson, the 19th Lord and tenth Baronet, in 1965.{{Historic Environment Scotland |desc=Craigievar Castle |num=GDL00114 |accessdate=1 July 2017}} Designed in the [[L Plan Castle|L-plan]],{{citation |last1=MacGibbon |first1=David |last2=Ross |first2=Thomas |title=The castellated and domestic architecture of Scotland from the twelfth to the eighteenth century |url=https://archive.org/stream/castellateddomes02macguoft#page/104/mode/2up/search/Craigievar |year=1887 |publisher=D. Douglas |page=104}} as was [[Muchalls Castle]], which is located in the same region, Craigievar is noted for its crafted [[plasterwork]] ceilings. Craigevar, [[Muchalls Castle]] and [[Glamis Castle]] are generally considered to have the three finest ceilings in Scotland.{{Cn|date=October 2024}} The [[Clan Forbes]] family was close friends of the [[Clan Burnett]] of Leys, who built both [[Crathes Castle]] and Muchalls Castle. The ceilings feature plaster figures of the [[Nine Worthies]] and other family emblems. ===19th century=== [[File:David Young Cameron - Craigievar Castle - B2001.12.17 - Yale Center for British Art.jpg|thumb|''Craigievar Castle'', [[David Young Cameron]], [[drypoint]], 1908]] [[File:Craigievar Castle SLNSW FL13814163.jpg|thumb|The castle c. 1907]] By the early 1800s, the tower had fallen into decay. Sir John Forbes had considered demolishing the tower and consulted the Aberdeen city architect [[John Smith (architect)|John Smith]], who advised against that course of action, stating the tower was: "one of the finest specimens in the Country of the age and style in which it was built."{{cite book|last=Miller|first=David G.|title=Tudor Johnny: City Architect of Aberdeen: The Life and Works of John Smith 1781–1852|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1quYSQAACAAJ|year=2007|publisher=Librario|isbn=978-1-904440-97-0|pages=129–130}} He decided to restore the building. Roof repairs were undertaken circa 1826; a timber base covered with slates was used. At about the same time, "the towers were altered and raised and a new entrance door was put in, which was subsequently restored to the original entrance" according to the records of the Aberdeenshire Council.{{cite web |title=Aberdeenshire HER - NJ50NE0005 - CRAIGIEVAR CASTLE |url=https://online.aberdeenshire.gov.uk/smrpub/master/detail.aspx?refno=NJ50NE0005 |publisher=Aberdeenshire Council |accessdate=16 September 2020}} Reconstruction of almost the entire top floor was also completed. The windows, external harling and pointing were replaced, and it is likely Smith also designed the gardener's cottage.{{cite web |title=Craigievar Castle, Canmore ID 17471 |url=http://canmore.rcahms.gov.uk/en/site/17471/details/craigievar+castle/ |publisher=RCAHMS |accessdate=18 November 2013 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203082832/http://canmore.rcahms.gov.uk/en/site/17471/details/craigievar+castle/ |archivedate=3 December 2013 |url-status=live }} The castle originally had more defensive elements including a walled courtyard with four round towers; only one of the round towers remains today. In the arched door to that round tower are preserved the carved initials of Sir Thomas Forbes, William Forbes' son. There is also a massive iron [[portcullis]] or gate covering the entrance door which is named a [[yett]]. According to the folklore of the area, the castle is haunted by one or more ghosts.{{cite web |title=Best of Britain > 10 Fairytale Scottish Castles |url=https://www.britainexpress.com/best/10-fairytale-scottish-castles.htm |publisher=Britain Express |accessdate=16 September 2020}}{{cite web |title=Haunted Scottish castles |date=5 October 2015 |url=https://www.scotsman.com/arts-and-culture/haunted-scottish-castles-1493527 |publisher=The Scotsman |accessdate=16 September 2020}} ===20th century=== The Forbes family also owned a large granite house at [[Fintray]] near [[Inverurie]], Aberdeenshire. This became the family's main residence for a number of years until the [[Second World War]]. During the war, Fintray House was used as a hospital for wounded Belgian soldiers.{{cite book|last=Forbes|first=Ewan|title=The aul' days|url=https://archive.org/details/auldaysforb00forb|url-access=registration|publisher=Aberdeen University Press|location=Aberdeen|year=1984|isbn=0-08-032415-0}} In 1963,{{cite web |title=Craigievar Castle |url=https://www.clan-forbes.org/craigievar-castle |publisher=Clan Forbes |accessdate=16 September 2020}} the family sold Craigievar estate to the [[National Trust for Scotland]], which took over operation.{{cite web |title=The pink Scottish castle said to have inspired Walt Disney |date=28 June 2018 |url=https://www.thevintagenews.com/2018/06/28/craigievar-castle/ |publisher=The Vintage News |accessdate=16 September 2020}} Since 1990, the estate has been a [[listed building]] of the Aberdeenshire Council. By the late 1970s, the castle interior boasted a [[Great Hall]] that has the [[House of Stuart|Stuart]] Arms over the fireplace; a musicians' gallery; secret staircase connecting the high tower to the Great Hall; Queen's Bedroom; servants' quarters and several plasterwork ceilings.{{citation |last=Jones |first=Nigel R. |title=Architecture of England, Scotland, and Wales |year=2005 |publisher=Greenwood |isbn=978-0-313-31850-4 |pages=85–87}} There was a collection of Forbes family portraits inside as well as a considerable quantity of Forbes furnishings dating to the 17th and 18th centuries. The castle also housed two original [[Henry Raeburn]] portraits complete with original receipts. ==21st century== [[File:CraigievarCastle.jpg|thumb|The castle, with new harling, in 2010]] Between November 2007 and 2009, the castle was closed for its exterior to be given a new [[harl]], returning it to what is believed to be a close equivalent of the harling put in place during the refurbishment of 1820.{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/scotland/north_east/8302858.stm|title=BBC NEWS - UK - Scotland - North East/N Isles - Castle in the pink after facelift|website=news.bbc.co.uk|date=12 October 2009 }} It was reopened to the public in April 2010.{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/scotland/north_east/8654763.stm|title=BBC News - Restored Craigievar Castle reopens to public|website=news.bbc.co.uk|date=30 April 2010 }} One report provided these specifics about the work and the state of the castle as of 2010:
The tower was renovated and rehabbed ... featuring a traditional lime-based alternative to concrete-based harling and returning the castle to what would have been its original shade of pink. The castle interior boasts a Great Hall that has the Stuart Arms over the fireplace; a musicians' gallery; a secret staircase connecting the high tower to the Great Hall; Queen's Bedroom; servants' quarters and several splendid plasterwork ceilings. The castle contains a collection of Forbes family portraits and furnishings dating to the 17th and 18th centuries.
No artificial lighting was ever added to the upper floors of the castle, so the artefacts would be viewed in the same natural light as they were during the previous centuries.{{Cite news |title=Scottish Castles {{!}} Best Castles In Scotland & Beyond {{!}} HighlandTitles |url=https://www.highlandtitles.com/blog/top-10-castles-in-scotland-and-beyond/#Craigievar_Castle |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200124034742/https://www.highlandtitles.com/blog/top-10-castles-in-scotland-and-beyond/#Craigievar_Castle |archive-date=2020-01-24 |access-date=2025-12-05 |work=Highland Titles |language=en-GB}} In 2019, a report provided this summary of the castle grounds:{{cite web |title=Cragievar Castle |date=31 December 1799 |url=https://www.parksandgardens.org/places/craigievar-castle |publisher=Parks and Gardens |accessdate=16 September 2020}}
Little remains of the 17th-century-designed landscape and the grounds around the Castle date from the late-18th and early-19th centuries. Further planting, particularly of ornamental conifers, was added at the end of the 19th century. In the 1930s a rock garden was created behind the coach house and, more recently, flower borders were added around the Castle and in the kitchen garden.
In early 2019, a volunteer discovered what is apparently the original door of the property, made of oak; it was replaced in 1825 and was considered to be missing until 2019. The door was subsequently restored and put on display.{{cite web |title=National Trust for Scotland opens door into past of Cragievar Castle with newest discovery |date=13 May 2019 |url=https://www.pressandjournal.co.uk/fp/news/aberdeen/1746793/national-trust-for-scotland-opens-door-into-past-of-cragievar-castle-with-newest-discovery/ |publisher=The Press & Journal |accessdate=16 September 2020}} By 2013, the castle, its grounds and an estate of over {{convert|200|acre|ha}} of adjoining farmland and woodland were in their 50th year as a property of the National Trust for Scotland. Visits to the castle were allowed from Easter, or from the first of April (whichever is the earlier) until the end of September. In 2018, the castle was open between April and June, on Fridays to Tuesdays for guided tours; the grounds were open throughout the year. The site received 24,072 visitors in 2019.{{cite web |title=ALVA - Association of Leading Visitor Attractions |url=https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 |website=www.alva.org.uk |accessdate=18 November 2020}} The National Trust continued to operate tours of the castle in 2019, but during 2020, the estate was closed due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the UK]]; upon reopening in July, visits were allowed only on the grounds for the rest of the season.{{cite web |title=Mixed picture for north-east National Trust attractions reopening|date=16 November 2016 |url=https://www.eveningexpress.co.uk/fp/news/local/mixed-picture-for-north-east-national-trust-attractions-reopening/ |publisher=Evening Express |accessdate=16 September 2020}}{{cite web |url=https://news.stv.tv/scotland/national-trust-to-open-dozens-of-outdoor-sites-to-the-public?top|title=National Trust to open dozens of outdoor sites to the public|publisher=STV |accessdate=16 September 2020|date=6 July 2020}} A September 2020 report states that the castle "holds a foremost place among the examples of what is known as the fourth or L period, from the form of ground plan upon which nearly all the Scottish castles of that date". The castle was closed to visitors for about two years while the exterior was properly restored by National Trust for Scotland. The exterior was coated in limewash, the most effective coating over stone walls in the local climate. It reopened at the end of May 2024.{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cd11lwj3lp5o.amp |title=Castle that inspired Walt Disney set to re-open |work=BBC News |date=28 May 2024 |access-date=5 August 2024 }} The castle relies on its windows for light, as there is no electricity in the rooms. The family had insisted in 1963 that the interiors not be changed, including artworks, decorative plaster work, panelling, and the lack of electricity for room lighting. The gift shop has a bit of electric lighting. Some members of the Forbes family, raised in the castle before the 1963 donation to Scotland, visit the castle in this decade of the 2020s. The exterior pink color was part of Aberdeen architect John Smith's 1826 makeover to "match the colour of the granite mouldings".{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/destinations/europe/united-kingdom/scotland/craigievar-scottish-castle-inspired-walt-disney/ |title=The 'strange and curious' Scottish castle that inspired Walt Disney |work=The Telegraph |first=Robin |last=McKelvie |date=5 September 2024 |access-date=5 August 2024 }} ==In popular culture== The castle is reputed to have been the inspiration for [[Walt Disney]]'s castle motif.{{cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/local/northeastscotlandnorthernisles/hi/people_and_places/history/newsid_8572000/8572293.stm |title=Craigievar Castle restoration |work=BBC News |date=23 March 2010}}{{cite web |url=http://news.stv.tv/north/129589-walt-disney-inspiring-castle-returned-to-fairytale-pink/|title=Walt Disney-inspiring castle returned to 'fairytale' pink |website=STV News |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190627220624/https://stv.tv/news/north/129589-walt-disney-inspiring-castle-returned-to-fairytale-pink/|archive-date=27 June 2019|date=12 October 2009}} This '''Fyvie Castle''' is a [[castle]] in the village of [[Fyvie]], near [[Turriff]] in [[Aberdeenshire]], Scotland. The earliest parts of the castle date from the 13th century, and it later passed through the hands of several prominent families, including the Prestons, Setons and Gordons. Since 1984 it has been owned and managed by the [[National Trust for Scotland]].

== History ==
The earliest parts of Fyvie Castle date from the 13th century – some sources claim it was built in 1211 by [[William the Lion]].  Fyvie was the site of an open-air court held by [[Robert the Bruce]], and [[Charles I of England|Charles I]] lived there as a child for 4 years.  Following the [[Battle of Otterburn]] in 1388, it ceased to function as a royal stronghold when it was granted to Henry Preston by Robert III. Instead, it fell into the possession of five successive families – ''Preston'', ''Meldrum'', ''Seton'', ''Gordon'' and ''Forbes-Leith'' – each of whom added a new tower to the castle. The oldest of these, the Preston Tower (located on the far right as one faces the main facade of Fyvie), dates to between 1390 and 1433. The Seton tower forms the entrance and was erected in 1599 by [[Alexander Seton, 1st Earl of Dunfermline|Alexander Seton]]. He commissioned the wheel staircase several years later. The Gordon Tower followed in 1777, and the Leith in 1890.

Inside, the castle stronghold features a wheel stair, a display of original arms and armour, and a collection of portraits, from artists such as [[Henry Raeburn]], [[Pompeo Batoni]] and [[Thomas Gainsborough]].

[[Manus O'Cahan's Regiment (English Civil War)|Manus O'Cahan]] and [[James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose|Montrose]] fought a battle against the Covenant Army at Fyvie Castle on 28 October 1644. The battlefield was added to the [[Inventory of Historic Battlefields in Scotland]] on 30 November 2011.<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=BTL22|desc=Battle of Fyvie|access-date=28 February 2019}}</ref> [[Anne Halkett]] stayed at the castle from 1650 to 1652 with the [[Charles Seton, 2nd Earl of Dunfermline|Countess of Dunfermline]]. During her stay, she treated wounded soldiers and local illnesses, and negotiated with the English major of a company of Commonwealth soldiers, as well as with three colonels, [[Robert Lilburne|Lilburne]], Fitts, and [[Robert Overton|Overton]].<ref>John Gough Nichols, [https://archive.org/details/autobiographyofa00halkrich/page/64/mode/2up ''Autobiography of the Lady Halkett'' (London, 1875), pp. 64-71]</ref>

The grounds and adjoining Fyvie Lake were landscaped in the 18th century by Col. William Gordon.  

The Scottish industrialist [[Alexander Forbes-Leith, 1st Baron Leith of Fyvie|Alexander Leith]] (later Baron Leith of Fyvie) bought the castle in 1885. His descendants sold it to the [[National Trust for Scotland]] in 1984.

To the east there is a walled garden where Scottish fruits are currently cultivated.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.scotlandsgardens.org/gardens/garden/b0c165cf-f672-41af-9322-99fc00b40f22 |title=Fyvie Castle - Scotland's Gardens |access-date=2015-08-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924095449/http://www.scotlandsgardens.org/gardens/garden/b0c165cf-f672-41af-9322-99fc00b40f22 |archive-date=2015-09-24 |url-status=dead }}</ref> There is evidence for two other walled gardens closer to the castle itself to its west and south.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://cameronarchaeology.com/doc/Fyvie_Castle_Environs_Project_final_draft_with_images.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2015-08-21 |archive-date=2016-02-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160205102556/http://cameronarchaeology.com/doc/Fyvie_Castle_Environs_Project_final_draft_with_images.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The one to the west appears on an estate plan of 1768.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Plan Of The Lands Of Fyvie And Surrounding Lands, Aberdeenshire {{!}} ScotlandsPlaces|url=https://scotlandsplaces.gov.uk/record/nrs/RHP11/plan-lands-fyvie-and-surrounding-lands-aberdeenshire/nrs#zoom=2&lat=2591.5&lon=4958.5&layers=B|access-date=2021-08-03|website=scotlandsplaces.gov.uk|language=en}}</ref>

== Ghostlore ==
Fyvie Castle is associated with a body of local ghostlore and traditional legends, many of which form part of its modern guided tours.<ref name="NTS">{{cite web |title=Fyvie Castle – Highlights |url=https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/fyvie-castle/highlights/castle |publisher=National Trust for Scotland |access-date=25 February 2026}}</ref>

According to tradition, the castle is subject to two curses. One relates to a sealed medieval dungeon, which legend holds would bring death to any intruder and blindness to his wife. Another, known as the “Curse of the Weeping Stones”, is traditionally attributed to the 13th-century seer [[Thomas the Rhymer]], and is said to explain why eldest sons of the families who owned Fyvie allegedly failed to inherit the estate. Of the three stones said to be involved in the curse, one is displayed in the Charter Room.<ref name="NTS" />

The castle is also said to be haunted by the “Green Lady”, identified with Lilias Drummond, wife of Alexander Seton. Legend maintains that her name was carved into a stone windowsill on the night of her husband’s remarriage, and that sightings of her ghost have been reported within the castle.<ref name="NTS" /><ref name="P&J2022">{{cite news |last=Ritchie |first=Gayle |title=Spooky stronghold: The ghosts, ‘weeping’ stones and secret chambers of Fyvie Castle |work=The Press and Journal |date=17 November 2022 |url=https://www.pressandjournal.co.uk/fp/entertainment/4960588/spooky-stronghold-fyvie-castle/ |access-date=25 February 2026}}</ref>

A further tradition reported in local press recounts that a woman’s skeleton discovered within a wall in the late 1920s was later reinterred after sightings of a “Grey Lady” were said to follow its removal.<ref name="P&J2022" />

== In the media ==
Fyvie Castle has featured in a number of British television programmes, such as Living TV's ''[[Most Haunted]]'' series 6<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.livingtv.co.uk/mosthaunted/214.php |title=LIVING : Most Haunted |access-date=2008-02-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070830064108/http://www.livingtv.co.uk/mosthaunted/214.php |archive-date=2007-08-30 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and STV's ''Castles of Scotland''.
The castle also played host of the setting of a children's gameshow on CBBC called ''[[Spook Squad]]'' in 2004. 2009 saw the publication of the children's fantasy novel, ''The Time-Tailor and the Fyvie Castle Witch Trials'', written by [[Deborah Leslie]]. The castle was also featured in the [[BBC]] documentary ''Castle Ghosts of Scotland'',<ref>[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0115843/ www.imdb.com]</ref> narrated by [[Robert Hardy]].

In recent years, the castle grounds have hosted a ''Fyvie Live'' music festival in the summer, which was headlined in 2011 by [[Beverley Knight]] and in 2012 by [[Sophie Ellis-Bextor]], then following a gap of several years, by [[The Shires (duo)|The Shires]] in 2017. Following the revival, it was announced that the event would take place again in 2018, with [[Ward Thomas (band)|Ward Thomas]] as the headline act. In August 2024 it also hosted re-enactors from all over the country to bring a re-enactment of the battle of Fyvie 1644.

Today, the castle is open to tourists between April and October. It is also a wedding venue.

'''Haddo House''' is a Scottish [[stately home]] located near [[Tarves, Aberdeenshire|Tarves]] in [[Aberdeenshire]], approximately {{convert|20|mi}} north of [[Aberdeen]] ({{gbmapping|NJ868347}}). Completed in 1732 to designs by [[William Adam (architect)|William Adam]], it was the former seat of the [[Marquess of Aberdeen and Temair|Earls and Marquesses of Aberdeen and Temair]] and has been owned by the [[National Trust for Scotland]] since 1979.

==Establishment and architectural style==
[[File:Dinner at Haddo House, 1884 by Alfred Edward Emslie.jpg|300px|thumb|right|''Dinner at Haddo House'', 1884 portrait by [[Alfred Edward Emslie]]]]
The Gordons, who later became the [[Marquess of Aberdeen and Temair|Earls of Aberdeen]] and [[Marquess of Aberdeen and Temair|Marquesses of Aberdeen]], lived on the site for more than 500 years.<ref name=TT>[http://www.ntseducation.org.uk/teachers/properties/haddo-house.html National Trust for Scotland] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071217200601/http://www.ntseducation.org.uk/teachers/properties/haddo-house.html |date=17 December 2007 }}</ref> Haddo House sits in or near the site of the old Kellie Castle, the family's previous dwelling which was burnt down by the [[Covenanters]]. Dating from 1732,<ref name=TT/> it was designed by [[William Adam (architect)|William Adam]] in the [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] [[Palladian architecture|Palladian]] style. The interior of the house is late [[Victorian architecture|Victorian]] in style, having undergone refurbishment in 1880 by Wright and Mansfield.<ref name=TT/> Haddo contains a large art collection, including a series of 85 castles by [[James Giles (painter)|James Giles]] and an early work by [[Claude Lorrain]].<ref>[http://www.aboutaberdeen.com/haddohouse.php aboutaberdeen.com]</ref>

==Gardens and designed landscape==
The grounds of Haddo House are included in the [[Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes in Scotland]] and were designated in 1987. The designed landscape is recognised as an outstanding example of 18th- and 19th-century landscape design, associated with [[William Adam (architect)|William Adam]], the artist [[James Giles (painter)|James Giles]], and [[George Hamilton-Gordon, 4th Earl of Aberdeen]]. It comprises an extensive country estate with large-scale parkland, woodland policies, avenues and water features, and makes a major contribution to the scenic character of the surrounding area.<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Haddo House
 |website=Trove
 |publisher=Historic Environment Scotland
 |url=https://www.trove.scot/designation/GDL00206
 |access-date=13 January 2026
}}</ref>

==Dinner service==
A specially made display cabinet contains the [[Cabot Commemorative State Dinner Service]]. The hand-painted porcelain service with twenty-four settings for an eight-course meal was made by members of the [[Woman's Art Association of Canada]] in 1897. The Canadian government declined to pay the CAD$1,000 asking price. It was purchased privately by members of the House and Senate of Canada and presented on 12 June 1898 to [[Ishbel Hamilton-Gordon, Marchioness of Aberdeen and Temair|Lady Aberdeen]] on the occasion of her husband, [[John Hamilton-Gordon, 1st Marquess of Aberdeen and Temair]], ending his term as Governor-General of Canada.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Cabot Commemorative State Service for Canada, 1897 - A History|page=3|publisher=Canadian Museum of History|url=http://www.historymuseum.ca/cmc/exhibitions/hist/cadeau/cahis03e.shtml|access-date=2014-07-14}}</ref>

==Peripheral buildings==
[[John Smith (architect)|John Smith]] did the design work for the kitchens and peripheral buildings in 1843. He returned there in 1845 and built the gatehouses at the North and South entrances. Constructed in coarse, rough granite, these single-storey buildings are in a Tudor style.<ref>{{cite book|last=Miller|first=David G.|title=Tudor Johnny: City Architect of Aberdeen: The Life and Works of John Smith 1781-1852|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1quYSQAACAAJ|year=2007|publisher=Librario|isbn=978-1-904440-97-0|page=348}}</ref>

==Prime ministerial residence==
Haddo House's most notable former resident was [[George Hamilton-Gordon, 4th Earl of Aberdeen]], who served as [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom]] from 1852–1855.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://heraldry-scotland.com/copgal/displayimage.php?album=6&pos=75 |title=The Heraldry Society of Scotland |access-date=21 December 2007 |archive-date=24 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181124162615/http://heraldry-scotland.com/copgal/displayimage.php?album=6&pos=75 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==World War II hospital==
Another notable period in its history was during World War II when the house became a maternity hospital for the evacuated mothers of Glasgow. Nearly 1,200 babies were born at Haddo Emergency Hospital, as it was known, and many of these 'Haddo Babies' still come back to visit.<ref>[http://www.nts.org.uk/NewsStory/940/ Search is on for Haddo babies], ''National Trust For Scotland'', 18 June 2010. Accessed 7 January 2012.</ref>

==Theatre==
The house has a small chapel attached. In the grounds is a theatre, Haddo House Hall, and rehearsal rooms, known as the Peatyards. Haddo House Choral & Operatic Society (HHCOS), a large and vibrant choral society formed in 1945, has its operations base there. For over sixty years it has been noted for its annual musical and operatic productions.<ref>{{cite web
 |last=Fraser
 |first=Peter
 |title=Haddo House Choral & Operatic Society
 |website=OperaScotland
 |year=2014
 |url=http://www.operascotland.org/person/8203/Haddo+House+C+%26+O+Society
 |access-date=13 January 2026
}}</ref>

==Damage by Storm Arwen==
In 2021, around 100,000 trees were destroyed during [[Storm Arwen]]. It is estimated that it will take a generation for the estate to return to its pre-storm way.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-north-east-orkney-shetland-59552325| title=Haddo House lost 100,000 trees during Storm Arwen| work=[[BBC News]]| date=6 December 2021| access-date=7 December 2021}}</ref>

7230524.extract: Pitmedden Garden is a garden near the village of Pitmedden, Aberdeenshire, Scotland. It is owned by the National Trust for Scotland. The garden dates from around 1675 and contains formal parterres, herbaceous borders, and an orchard. It is open to the public.

'''Pitmedden Garden''' is a garden near the village of [[Pitmedden]], [[Aberdeenshire]], Scotland. It is owned by the [[National Trust for Scotland]].<ref name="NTS">{{cite web |title=Pitmedden Garden |url=https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/pitmedden-garden |website=National Trust for Scotland |access-date=10 January 2026}}</ref> The garden dates from around 1675<ref name="Buxbaum1989">{{cite book |last=Buxbaum |first=Tim |title=Scottish Garden Buildings: From Food to Folly |publisher=Mainstream Publishing |year=1989 |isbn=1-85158-113-8 |page=30}}</ref> and contains formal [[parterre]]s, herbaceous borders, and an orchard. It is open to the public.<ref name="NTS"/>

== History == 

The earliest recording of a house on the property was in the early 15th century by the Panton family.<ref name=HES>{{cite web |author1=Peter McGowan Associates |title=Pitmedden Historic Landscape Survey Summary |url=https://i.rcahms.gov.uk/canmore-pdf/WP00007729.pdf |website=Historic Environment Scotland |access-date=10 May 2026 |format=PDF |date=March 2007}}</ref>  By 1603, there was now a garden and estate including a tower, [[Fortification|fortalice]], orchards, [[dovecote]], and water meadows.<ref name=HES />{{rp|3}}

The Seton family owned the site from 1603 to 1893.<ref name=HES />{{rp|1}}  Sir Alexander Seton and Dame Margaret Lauder, his wife, took possession in 1658,<ref name=HES /> established a house and garden at the site in 1675.<ref>{{cite book |title=Hudson's Historic Houses and Gardens |publisher=Hudson}}</ref> The original house, together with the garden plans, was largely destroyed by fire in 1807.<ref>{{cite web |title=Aberdeenshire HER – NJ82NE0034 – Pitmedden House and Garden |publisher=Aberdeenshire Council |url=https://online.aberdeenshire.gov.uk/smrpub/master/detail.aspx?Authority=ASH&refno=NJ82NE0034 |date=8 January 2021 |access-date=13 November 2022}}</ref>

By 1858 the estate size had changed with the introduction of turnpike roads.<ref name=HES />  Whilst owned by the Setons, it appears the estate was more managed by tenants.<ref name=HES />{{rp|3}}

The house was later occupied in the 1800s by shipping owner and politician [[George Thompson (shipowner)|George Thompson]].  

About 1893 or 1894,<ref name=HES />{{rp|1}} the house and garden went to Major James Keith.  In 1952, the year before his death, Keith gifted the garden to the [[National Trust for Scotland]].<ref name=GfS>{{cite web |title=Pitmedden, Aberdeenshire |url=https://www.scottish-places.info/towns/townfirst4011.html |website=Gazetteer for Scotland |access-date=5 January 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=What's the time, Major Keith? |url=https://www.nts.org.uk/stories/whats-the-time-major-keith |publisher=National Trust for Scotland |access-date=10 May 2026 |date=1 September 2017}}</ref>  Much of the estate lands were sold to provide ongoing maintenance capital.<ref name=HES />

== Design==

The garden is noted for its geometric parterres, which vary in shape from a [[thistle]] to [[Sir Alexander Seton, 1st Baronet|Sir Alexander Seton]]'s coat of arms. Pitmedden also has several long, varied borders which run along the garden walls.

The 20th century restoration based three of the [[parterre]] sections on the 1647 plan of Holyrood Palace by Gordon of Rothiemay, and the fourth section represents a memorial to Alexander Seton and his father John Seton.<ref name="Buxbaum1989"/>

When handed over in 1952, the grounds included a {{convert|9|ft}} 1675 [[sundial]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article187444533 |title=Annual Scottish Review: The North Countrie |newspaper=[[Warwick Daily News]] |issue=10,415 |location=Queensland, Australia |date=26 December 1952 |access-date=10 May 2026 |page=2 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> 

Along with more than 200 fruit trees and {{convert|6|mi}} of hedges, there is a Museum of Farming Life.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pitmedden Garden: About this place |url=https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/pitmedden-garden |website=National Trust for Scotland |access-date=10 May 2026}}</ref>

Environment Scotland|num=LB48775|short=yes}} }} | references = | footnotes = }}'''Mar Lodge''' is a sporting lodge {{convert|5|mi|km|0|abbr=off}} to the west of [[Braemar]] and the principal building on the [[Mar Lodge Estate]] in [[Aberdeenshire]], [[Scotland]]. It was built in 1895, replacing an earlier building, by [[Alexander Duff, 1st Duke of Fife]]. ==Location== [[File:Marlodge from linnofdeeroad 03SEP06.jpg|thumb|Mar Lodge from Linn of Dee Road|left]] Mar Lodge is a sporting lodge built for the use of the [[Alexander Duff, 1st Duke of Fife|Duke]] and [[Louise, Princess Royal|Duchess of Fife]]. It is located about {{convert|4|mi|km|0|abbr=off}} to the west of [[Braemar]] and is accessed from the [[Linn of Dee]] road, over the [[Victoria Bridge (Mar Lodge Estate)|Victoria Bridge]], a lattice girder structure built across the [[River Dee, Aberdeenshire|River Dee]] in 1905. ==History== There have been three buildings known as Mar Lodge. The first, originally known as Dalmore House, was built in the 18th century by [[William Duff, 1st Earl Fife|William Duff, Baron Braco]],Dixon & Green close to the site of the present Lodge.{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=LB48775|desc=Mar Lodge Estate, Mar Lodge including Garden Wall|cat=B|access-date=21 March 2019}} Lord Braco had acquired the Dalmore estate some time between 1730 and 1737 from the Mackenzie lairds of Dalmore, and by the end of the 18th century the Duff family also owned the lands of [[Allanaquoich]], Auchindryne and [[Inverey]]Wyness The Duffs owned huge swaths of land in addition to the estate as the heads of many [[Barons in Scotland|Scottish Feudal Baronies]], including [[Scottish Feudal Barony of MacDuff|MacDuff]], named for [[James Duff, 2nd Earl Fife]].{{Cite book |last=Mosley |first=Charles |title=Burke's Peerage Baronetage & Knightage: Clan Chiefs, Scottish Feudal Barons |publisher=Burke's Peerage and Gentry LLC |edition=107th Edition, Volumes I-III |location=Wilmington, Delaware |pages=1021, 1759}}{{Cite book |title=The General Register of Sasines |year=1982 |edition=Book 1001, Folio 70 |location=Edinburgh, UK: Public Records Office, Register House |pages=76}} The building was damaged in the "[[Muckle Spate (1829)|Muckle Spate]]" ("great flood") of 1829,{{cite web| url=http://www.historic-scotland.gov.uk/cairngorms.pdf| title=A selection of the Cairngorms National Park's architectural heritage| publisher=Historic Scotland| accessdate=7 February 2009}} and later demolished.{{cite web| url=http://www.scottish-places.info/features/featurefirst3920.html | title=Overview of Mar Lodge (Corriemulzie Cottage)| publisher=[[Gazetteer for Scotland]]| accessdate=7 February 2009}} The lodges served as the seat for the 5th-7th Barons of MacDuff.{{Cite web |date=September 13, 2023 |title=The Historic Seats of the Barons of MacDuff |url=https://www.baronyofmacduff.org/blank-page-5 |access-date=September 13, 2023 |website=www.thebaronyofmacduff.org}} === Corriemulzie Cottage === The 2nd Mar Lodge, colloquially known as Corriemulzie Cottage or 'New' Mar Lodge, was built near [[Corriemulzie|Linn of Corriemulzie]] at the top of [[Places, place names, and structures on Mar Lodge Estate#Mar Lodge Brae|Mar Lodge Brae]]. It was a very 'Victorian' building with architectural detailing such as prominent use of lattice work (still visible on the 'Stag Ballroom') and tree-trunk supports (visible in the veranda of the old bar at the rear of Mar Lodge) being reused in the construction of the next Mar Lodge. It was destroyed by fire on the 14th of June 1895. === The present lodge === [[File:Victoria-Bridge,-Inverey-02.jpg|thumb|The Mar Lodge Gatehouse, as seen from [[Victoria Bridge (Mar Lodge Estate)|Victoria Bridge]]|left]] The 3rd Mar Lodge was built between 1895 and 1898 for the [[Alexander Duff, 1st Duke of Fife]] and his wife [[Louise, Princess Royal and Duchess of Fife|Princess Louise, Princess Royal and Duchess of Fife]]. The foundation stone was laid by her grandmother [[Victoria of the United Kingdom|Queen Victoria]] on 15 October 1895.{{cite web| url=http://www.rampantscotland.com/stay/blstay_mar.htm| title=Mar Lodge, Braemar|publisher=Rampant Scotland|accessdate=7 February 2009}} {{Blockquote|The architect was [[Alexander Marshall Mackenzie]] of Aberdeen (1848-1933) who, at the express request of the Duchess—H.R.H. Princess Louise, in the Elizabethan style of architecture.|Wyness, Fenton}} An old postcard shows the original veranda and drive alignment that allowed horse-drawn carriages arriving from [[Braemar]] to pull up at the main door.{{Citation needed|date=November 2014}} The 3rd Mar Lodge was extensively damaged by a fire while being renovated in 1991, but was rebuilt. It was converted into holiday flats and retains many of the grand features of its heyday as a hunting lodge. The ballroom has 2,435 red deer stags heads lining the walls and ceiling.{{cite web|url=http://www.braemarscotland.co.uk/history/index.htm |title=History |publisher=Braemar Guide |accessdate=7 February 2009 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090131224221/http://www.braemarscotland.co.uk/history/index.htm |archivedate=January 31, 2009 }} [[Mar Lodge Estate]] became a [[National Trust for Scotland]] property in 1995. ==Stag Ballroom== A ballroom was constructed for estate staff balls, required by the need for segregation between master and servant which dominated the period. Built near to the second Mar Lodge at Corriemulzie, it was moved to the present site in 1898. A large timber building in the estate red, it has distinctive lattice trellising, an original Victorian ventilation system and unusual cast iron bracers on stone plinths supporting the walls. Internally the building remains virtually in its original state and contains over 2,000 stags skulls.{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=LB50769|desc=Mar Lodge Estate, The Ballroom|cat=B|access-date=22 March 2019}} Image:mar-lodge-foundation-stone.jpg | The foundation stone Image:marlodge_interior_01.jpg | Interior of Mar Lodge Image:marlodge_interior_02.jpg | Interior of Mar Lodge Image:Marlodgeantlers.jpg|Ballroom with thousands of antlers ==St Ninian's Chapel== {{main|St Ninian's Chapel, Braemar}} [[File:Braemar, Mar Lodge Estate, St Ninian's Chapel - exterior 08.JPG|thumb|150px|St Ninian's Chapel]] St Ninian's Chapel stands immediately adjacent to Mar Lodge and was originally the private chapel of the owners of Mar Lodge. The 1st Duke of Fife and his family are buried in the chapel.{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=LB50768|desc=Mar Lodge Estate, St Ninian's Chapel (Scottish Episcopal Church)|cat=B|access-date=22 March 2019|fewer-links=yes}} ==Sources== * {{Citation | title=[[Royal Valley : The Story Of The Aberdeenshire Dee]] | first=Fenton | last=Wyness | publisher=Alex P. Mar Lodge Estate is a highland estate in western Aberdeenshire, Scotland, which has been owned and managed by the National Trust for Scotland (NTS) since 1995. Its principal building, Mar Lodge, is about 4 miles (6.4 km) west of the village of Braemar. The estate is recognised as one of the most important nature conservation landscapes in the British Isles and occupies nearly 8% of the Cairngorms National Park, covering 29,340 hectares (72,500 acres). The natural heritage value of the estate is reflected by the fact that much of it is designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI), a Special Area of Conservation (SAC) and a Special Protection Area (SPA). The entire estate has been classified as a national nature reserve since May 2017, and is designated a Category II protected area by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Extreme weather conditions are experienced across the estate, especially on the plateau. Landslides, avalanches and floods alter the landscape and give it an interesting geomorphology. The estate is characterised by rounded granite Cairngorm mountains to the north, with deep corries and crags down to the valley floor. Spectacular glacial breaches include the Lairig Ghru and Lairig an Laoigh. To the south west are the more open, rolling hills of the Geldie. Waters flowing from the mountains become the headwaters of the River Dee.
The estate is popular with hill walkers, containing 14 Munros, and 4 of the 5 highest mountains in Scotland, including Britain’s second highest mountain, Ben Macdui. A car park and toilet facilities are provided by NTS close to the waterfall of the Linn of Dee, which is the main access point to the area. Public access to the estate for outdoor activities such as hillwalking, climbing and wild camping is permitted by the general right to responsible access that applies to all land in Scotland under the Scottish outdoor access code.
