'''Mar Lodge Estate''' is a highland estate in western [[Aberdeenshire]], [[Scotland]], which has been owned and managed by the [[National Trust for Scotland]] (NTS) since 1995. Its principal building, [[Mar Lodge]], is about {{convert|4|mi|km}} west of the village of [[Braemar]]. The estate is recognised as one of the most important nature conservation landscapes in the British Isles and occupies nearly 8% of the [[Cairngorms National Park]], covering {{convert|29340|ha|acre}}.<ref name="SNH-NNR">{{cite web|url=http://www.nnr-scotland.org.uk/mar-lodge-estate/|title=Mar Lodge Estate|publisher=Scottish Natural Heritage|accessdate=2018-02-06}}</ref> The natural heritage value of the estate is reflected by the fact that much of it is designated as a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI), a [[Special Area of Conservation]] (SAC) and a [[Special Protection Area]] (SPA).<ref name="whole_estate_forest_plan_2012">''Whole Estate Forest Plan'', National Trust for Scotland, 2012</ref> The entire estate has been classified as a [[National nature reserve (Scotland)|national nature reserve]] since May 2017,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nts.org.uk/What-we-do/Article/Scotlandas-Newest-National-Nature-Reserves/|title=Scotland's Newest National Nature Reserves|publisher=National Trust for Scotland|date=2017-04-17|accessdate=2018-02-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180208004246/https://www.nts.org.uk/What-we-do/Article/Scotlandas-Newest-National-Nature-Reserves/|archive-date=8 February 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> and is designated a [[Protected area#IUCN Protected Area Management Categories|Category II]] [[protected areas of Scotland|protected area]] by the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]].<ref name=planet>{{cite web|url=https://www.protectedplanet.net/555638750|title=Mar Lodge Estate|publisher=Protected Planet|accessdate=14 February 2021}}</ref>

Extreme weather conditions are experienced across the estate, especially on the plateau. Landslides, avalanches and floods alter the landscape and give it an interesting [[geomorphology]].<ref name="case"/> The estate is characterised by rounded [[granite]] [[Cairngorms|Cairngorm mountains]] to the north, with deep [[cirque|corrie]]s and crags down to the valley floor. Spectacular [[Glacier#Glacial valleys|glacial breaches]] include the [[Lairig Ghru]] and [[Lairig an Laoigh]]. To the south west are the more open, rolling hills of the [[River Geldie|Geldie]]. Waters flowing from the mountains become the headwaters of the [[River Dee, Aberdeenshire|River Dee]].

The estate is popular with [[hillwalking|hill walkers]], containing 14 [[Munro]]s, and 4 of the 5 highest mountains in Scotland, including Britain’s second highest mountain, [[Ben Macdui]]. A car park and toilet facilities are provided by NTS close to the waterfall of the [[Linn of Dee]], which is the main access point to the area.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nts.org.uk/visit/places/mar-lodge-estate|title=Mar Lodge Estate|publisher=National Trust for Scotland|accessdate=14 September 2020}}</ref> Public access to the estate for outdoor activities such as [[hillwalking]], [[climbing]] and wild [[camping]] is permitted by the general [[Freedom to roam#Scotland|right to responsible access]] that applies to all land in Scotland under the [[Scottish outdoor access code]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.outdooraccess-scotland.scot/|title=Scottish Outdoor Access Code|publisher=Scottish Natural Heritage|accessdate=2018-05-03}}</ref>

==Flora and fauna==
The estate contains examples of remnants of the ancient [[Caledonian Forest|Caledonian pine forest]], [[Moorland#Heather moorland|heather moorland]], [[juniper]] scrub and a part of the high Cairngorm plateau. It supports important populations of [[red grouse]], [[wader]]s and [[Bird of prey|raptors]].<ref name="nts">{{cite web| url=http://www.marlodgeestate.org.uk/| title=Mar Lodge Estate| publisher=[[National Trust for Scotland]]| accessdate=7 February 2009}}</ref>

The Caledonian pine forest is home to [[red squirrels]], [[pine marten]]s, [[wood ant]]s and birds such as the [[black grouse]], [[Scottish crossbill]] and [[parrot crossbill]], which are all rare or absent across most of Britain. The higher areas on the Cairngorm plateau host breeding populations of [[dotterel]], [[snow bunting]]s and [[ptarmigan]], and is also the largest area of [[arctic-alpine|arctic-alpine flora]] in Britain.<ref name="SNH-NNR"/>

==Built environment==
[[File:Mar_Lodge_Estate_-_Corrour_Bothy_'toilet_extension'_(21_August_2007)_(069).jpg|thumb|right|Corrour Bothy on Mar Lodge Estate, showing the toilet block extension]]
The architectural importance of the estate is reflected in the fact that there are 5 listed buildings including [[Mar Lodge]], which was built in 1895 by the [[Alexander Duff, 1st Duke of Fife|Duke of Fife]]. The ballroom has 2,435 red deer stags heads lining the walls and ceiling. The lodge was severely damaged by a fire in 1991 but rebuilt soon thereafter. It has since been converted into holiday flats and retains many of the grand features of its heyday as a hunting lodge.<ref name="history"/>

Six hunting lodges were constructed on the estate to allow shooting parties to be accommodated away from the main Mar Lodge building.  Only one, Derry Lodge, remains intact, although it is now in a dilapidated condition.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://canmore.org.uk/site/81561/derry-lodge|title=Derry Lodge|publisher=Canmore - National Record of the Historic Environment|accessdate=2018-02-06}}</ref> In 2016 NTS submitted plans to renovate the lodge to provide hostel accommodation: as the lodge is located 6 km from the nearest road at Linn of Dee this hostel would be accessible only by foot or bicycle.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.pressandjournal.co.uk/fp/news/aberdeenshire/949663/plans-lodged-to-transform-derelict-hunting-lodge-in-aberdeenshire-wilderness-into-hostel/
|title=Plans lodged to transform derelict hunting lodge in Aberdeenshire wilderness into hostel|newspaper=Press and Journal|date=2016-06-17|accessdate=2018-02-06}}</ref>

The estate includes land which has a number of national and international natural heritage designations, and is one of the country's largest areas of [[Scheduled Ancient Monument]]s and archaeological sites.<ref name="nts"/>

In 2006 the Cairngorms National Park Authority approved a planning application from the [[Mountain Bothies Association]] (MBA) to extend [[Corrour Bothy]] to install a wood-burning stove and add a toilet block to improve facilities for visitors.<ref>Andrew Tait, [https://archive.org/details/ReportOnCalledInPlanningApplication_CorrourBothyToiletExtension Corrour Bothy Toilet Extension], Cairngorms National Park Authority, 11 August 2006</ref> In January 2023 [[Places, place names, and structures on Mar Lodge Estate#Ruighe Ealasaid|Ruighe Ealasaid]] opened as an additional bothy on the estate, following two years of work by the MBA to bring a formerly derelict building back into use.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.scotsman.com/news/national/new-bothy-for-walkers-opens-deep-in-the-cairngorms-3978011|title=A new bothy has opened for walkers deep in the Cairngorms after voluteers spent two years renovating the derelict shieling|newspaper=The Scotsman|date=7 January 2023|accessdate=26 July 2023}}</ref>

==History==
Mar Lodge Estate is the largest remnant of the historic [[Earl of Mar|Earldom of Mar]].  Following the participation of [[John Erskine, 6th Earl of Mar|John "''Bobbing John''" Erskine, 6th Earl of Mar]] in the [[Jacobite Rising of 1715]] the estate was forfeited in 1716, which brought an end to the essentially feudal landholding system practiced in the Earldom of Mar, although the process of resolving the forfeiture of 1716 took many years. The next owners of the estate were [[James Erskine, Lord Grange]], brother of the Earl of Mar, and [[David Erskine, Lord Dun]].

Dalmore, the westernmost part was bought by the astute entrepreneur [[William Duff, 1st Earl Fife|William Duff of Dipple]], between 1730 and 1737.<ref>{{cite book| title=Royal Valley – The Story of the Aberdeenshire Dee| first=Fenton| last=Wyness| year=1968}}</ref> This formed the nucleus of Mar Estate. In the years that followed, the many minor lairdships surrounding the two large estates of Invercauld and Mar were gradually absorbed by one or the other, until they were the only two estates in Braemar.<ref name="history">{{cite web|url=http://www.braemarscotland.co.uk/history/index.htm |title=History |publisher=Braemar Guide |accessdate=7 February 2009 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090131224221/http://www.braemarscotland.co.uk/history/index.htm |archivedate=31 January 2009 }}</ref>

In the 19th century the estate moved towards being used primarily for recreational shooting and fishing with the building of the Hunting Lodges of Derry Lodge, Geldie Lodge and Bynack Lodge. The [[hamlet (place)|hamlet]] of [[Inverey]] is the only survivor of the estate [[Highland clearances|clearance]] – not counting the village of [[Braemar]] part of which was also very much part of Mar Estate well into the 20th century. In 1879 [[Alexander Duff, 1st Duke of Fife|Alexander William George Duff]] succeeded his father James becoming the 6th Earl Fife. At this time the Earl owned huge swaths of land in addition to the estate as the head of many [[Barons in Scotland|Scottish Feudal Baronies]], including [[Scottish Feudal Barony of MacDuff|MacDuff]], named for [[James Duff, 2nd Earl Fife]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mosley |title=Vol. I |year=2003 |pages=1021, 1759}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=The General Register of Sasines |year=1982 |edition=Book 1001, Folio 70 |location=Edinburgh, UK: Public Records Office, Register House |pages=76}}</ref> In 1889 he married the [[Louise, Princess Royal|Princess Royal]] and was made 1st [[Duke of Fife]].  Following his death in 1912 the estate was managed by [[trustees]], later passing to [[Princess Alexandra, Duchess of Fife]].

Between 1942 and 1944, Company 25, of the 2nd Forestry District, of the [[Canadian Forestry Corps]] operated the Canadian camp,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://theuplandofmar.squarespace.com/canadian-camp/|title=Canadian Camp|publisher=The Upland of Mar|accessdate=2018-02-06}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> a lumber camp on the land east of Lui Bridge on both sides of the road, and set about cutting down trees and processing them into lumber to support the war effort.

In 1959 [[Alexander Ramsay of Mar|Alexander Ramsay, Lord and Baron of Braemar]] inherited the estate from his aunt. In 1962 the Mar Lodge Estate was briefly owned by the Ashdale Property Company,<ref name="Dawson">Hugh Dawson, ''A Guide to the Chapel of Saint Ninian, Mar Lodge, Braemar. The Scottish Episcopal Church'', Braemar 2015</ref> who then sold it to the Swiss Panchaud family, in 1962.  The brothers Gerald and John Panchaud<ref name="Dawson"/> ran the estate as a commercial sporting venture and the Lodge as a hotel. Vehicle tracks were constructed throughout the estate, including one leading close to the summit of [[Beinn a' Bhùird]] which was constructed for a proposed skiing development.<ref name="case">{{cite web| url=http://www.ntseducation.org.uk/students/case-mar.html| title=Case Study – Mar Lodge| publisher=[[National Trust for Scotland]]| accessdate=7 February 2009| url-status=dead| archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080819181631/http://www.ntseducation.org.uk/students/case-mar.html| archivedate=19 August 2008}}</ref> The Panchauds also started the construction of a ski centre on the hill behind Mar Lodge.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://theuplandofmar.squarespace.com/mar-lodge-ski-centre|title=Mar Lodge ski centre|publisher=The Upland of Mar|accessdate=2018-02-06}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

In 1989 the estate was bought by Mar Lodge Estate Inc., a company owned by the German-American entrepreneur [[John Kluge]], which ran the estate for sporting purposes, with a greater emphasis on sensitive land management and improvement of facilities and buildings. Renovation of the Lodge was interrupted by a fire in 1991 and finally completely in 1993.<ref name="case"/>

On 30 June 1995 Mar Lodge Estate was acquired by the [[National Trust for Scotland]]. The Trust did not have the necessary money and required substantial financial assistance from both private & public organisations to fund the purchase.<ref>Crofts, Roger (2026), ''Scottish Natural Heritage: An Insider's View'', Tippermuir Books Limited, [[Perth, Scotland|Perth]], pp. 151 - 155, {{isbn|9781913836559}}</ref> The ''Easter Charitable Trust'' made a conditional offer of £4.5 million, and the [[Heritage Lottery Fund]] offered more-than £10 million.<ref name="hlf_2015">''HLF Major Grants - The First 100'', BOP Consulting, 2015</ref> £1.5 million of the funds raised went towards the purchase, and more-than £8 million went as an endowment, with [[NatureScot|Scottish Natural Heritage]] (SNH) entering into a 25-year Management Agreement, a 5-year Management Plan, and a 1-year Costed Capital Project Programme (renewed annually) with the Trust as frameworks to guide the provision of further public money. The purchase was completed in the knowledge that SNH would be an "active partner in managing the Estate".<ref name="SNH/01/7/3">{{cite work|title=Mar Lodge Estate (review) of Scottish Natural Heritage (Management Agreement) with the National Trust for Scotland (1995-2000)|publisher=Scottish Natural Heritage|date=2001}}</ref>

At the time there was much speculation that the [[Charles, Prince of Wales|Prince Charles]], [[Duke of Rothesay]] was behind the donation, however it was later discovered that Ann Marie Salvesen, a publicity-shy member of the [[Christian Salvesen]] shipping and distribution dynasty had anonymously donated £4.5m to assist with the purchase.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.independent.co.uk/environment/mystery-of-donor-who-saved-mar-lodge-is-solved-668188.html| title=Mystery of donor who saved Mar Lodge is solved| author=Paul Kelbie| date=25 January 2002|work=The Independent |location=UK| accessdate=7 February 2009}}{{dead link|date=August 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

==Conservation management==
[[File:Mar_Lodge_Estate_-_Making_Tracks_(28_July_2010)_(34).jpg|thumb|right|Track leading west from Luibeg to the edge of the Caledonian pinewood on Mar Lodge Estate]]
Following the purchase of the estate by the National Trust for Scotland, the report ''Mar Lodge Estate: Landscape Assessment Study'', commissioned jointly by the Trust and Scottish Natural Heritage, was published in 1996. The study was a detailed assessment of the landscape character of Mar Lodge Estate that considered the "pressures and opportunities for change in the landscape" whilst assessing "the sensitivity of the landscape to change" and included the recommendation of several conservation objectives (including the reiteration of existing Trust objectives) and principles to guide how the landscape of Mar Lodge Estate "may be conserved, enhanced or restructured".<ref name="landscape_assessment_1996">[https://archive.org/details/MarLodgeEstateLandscape_Assessment ''Mar Lodge Estate : Landscape Assessment Study''], Turnbull Jeffrey Partnership, 1996</ref> The primary aim of the study was to provide enough detailed information about the landscape of the estate to inform and shape an estate management plan. The resulting plan included the following principles:
* Alignment with the 'Unna Principles'.
* Advocacy of the 'long walk in'.
* Recognition that the Caledonian pinewoods were a "prime habitat for conservation".
* Intention to let the Caledonian pinewoods "expand its range by natural regeneration to create a self-sustaining woodland" without "fencing, [[tree planting]] or use of fertilisers".<ref name="landscape_assessment_1996" />
* Intention that "woodland expansion will be achieved by a substantial reduction in deer numbers".

A major objective of the National Trust for Scotland is to conserve the "wild land" quality on the Estate. The 1996 Landscape Assessment Study contained a number of proposals aiming to achieve these objectives.<ref name="landscape_assessment_1996"/>
* Dissuading and restricting use of existing vehicle tracks and the non-maintenance and restoration of hill-tracks.
* A gradual withdrawal of mechanical and wheeled vehicles (including bicycles - see below) from the core area.
* A presumption against large-scale recreational events on NTS countryside properties
* Educational and interpretation programmes promoting NTS's policy on wild land to visitors, which would outline concepts such as the 'long walk in' ... and provide advice on 'minimal impact'. 
The report also suggested removal of man-made elements such as sign posts, footbridges and bothies could be considered where they were "non-essential" to the management of the estate.

===Pinewood regeneration===
Native woodland is considered a prime habitat for conservation, and it is an objective of the National Trust for Scotland to encourage the [[Caledonian Forest|Caledonian pinewood]] to expand its range by natural regeneration.  The management plan envisaged that this expansion would be achieved by natural regeneration without the use of fencing, and would thus be achieved by a "substantial reduction in deer numbers and without resorting to additional fencing, tree planting or use of fertilizers". It was recognised that this would be a long-term process, and monitoring was recommended in order to assess whether measures to "kick-start" the process should be undertaken.<ref name="landscape_assessment_1996"/> When the Trust acquired Mar Lodge Estate, more than 3500 red deer roamed the estate and they set themselves the target to reduce that to 1600 by the year 2000.<ref>[https://www.independent.co.uk/news/heritage-a-fresh-start-in-the-land-where-eagles-dare-1240670.html ''Heritage: A fresh start in the land where eagles dare''], Independent, 21 September 1997</ref> Good practice would suggest that, without fencing the deer population must be reduced to the low single-digits per square kilometre.<ref name="johnston_2000">Laughton Johnston, ''Scotland's Nature in Trust'', T & AD Poyser, 2000</ref>

The Trust failed in its objective to reduce the deer population of the estate to 1600 by the year 2000. Scottish Natural Heritage considered that this failure was "despite strenuous efforts" and that the reason "for the shortfall would appear to be an underestimate of the original population size by as much as 20%", which resulted in the estimated deer population of 2700 in (year) 2000,<ref name="SNH/01/7/3"/> however it has been argued that efforts to reduce numbers were hampered by a reliance of traditional [[deer stalking]] practices, this being a stipulation of the Easter Trust funding.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://parkswatchscotland.co.uk/2018/12/27/the-royal-family-land-mis-management-and-the-cairngorms-national-park/|title=The Royal Family, land mis-management and the Cairngorms National Park|date=2018-12-27|author=Nick Kempe|website=parkswatchscotland.co.uk|accessdate=2019-03-08}}</ref> By 2011 the deer population was estimated as 1700, and thus in line with the original target,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nts.org.uk/site/docs/news/marlodgefinal_complete_18-11-11.pdf|title=Report for the board of the National Trust for Scotland into the management of deer, woodland and moorland at Mar Lodge Estate|publisher=Mar Lodge Independent Review Panel|date=November 2011|accessdate=2018-02-08}}</ref> although neighbouring estates had expressed concern that the reduction was impacting deer numbers on their estates, and hence the viability of their sporting businesses.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/scottish-news/top-gamekeeper-quits-famous-estate-1078238|title=Top gamekeeper quits famous estate over deer slaughter|newspaper=Daily Record|date=2012-07-01|accessdate=2018-02-08}}</ref>

Forest regeneration had not been as successful as hoped, which the trust ascribed to the delay in reducing deer numbers to the target level.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-north-east-orkney-shetland-14523760|title=Mar Lodge faces SNH penalty over forest regeneration|work=BBC News|date=2011-08-14|accessdate=2018-02-08}}</ref> The original plan of avoiding any fencing was thus altered, with the estate being divided into two zones (a moorland zone and a regeneration zone), with some fencing separating the two.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nts.org.uk/Downloads/Properties/wefp_1_web.pdf|title=Mar Lodge Estate Forest Plan 2012-2032|publisher=National Trust for Scotland|accessdate=2018-02-08}}</ref>

===Tracks===
[[File:Mar Lodge Estate - Making Tracks (22JUL09).jpg|thumb|right|The former bulldozed vehicle hill-track in Glen Derry on Mar Lodge Estate, looking towards Derry Lodge]]
In 1997, in line with the objectives and policies of the Trust to enhance the wild land quality and the 'long walk in' they began track removal work on Beinn a Bhuird.<ref name="jmt_51">''Covering Tracks'', Shaila Rao, John Muir Trust Journal, Number 51, Autumn 2011</ref> This vehicle hill-track had been extended from the head of Glen Quoich using a bulldozer over eight-weeks in 1966.<ref>Burke, John, ''Road to the Top'', Scottish Field, 1968</ref> The Trust found itself "in new territory, where the best and sometimes only advice it can get is from the experience of its own staff as they pioneer new techniques". These techniques comprised a three-stage process of (1) lifting vegetation that had naturally colonised the spoil; (2) using the spoil to re-grade the course of the vehicle hill-track, effectively blending the course of the vehicle hill-track back into the hill-side; and (3) replanting the vegetation lifted from the spoil leaving the width of a footpath unplanted. The re-vegetation was "supplemented by plants collected from densely vegetated areas within 50 metres of the track ... [and] plate-sized turfs of species such as heather and blaeberry".<ref name="jmt_51" /> The results were reviewed favourably by hillwalking publication [[The Angry Corrie]].<ref name=tac51>{{cite web|url=https://the-angry-corrie.000webhostapp.com/tac51/swingsan.htm|title=Swings, and the inevitable roundabout (hill tracks)|publisher=The Angry Corrie|date=September 2001|accessdate=2018-02-15}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

The 1996 Landscape Assessment had recommended the removal and revegetation of the majority of the tracks on the estate, including the one leading west from Luibeg to the edge of the Caledonian pinewood. In 2002 this track was re-engineered using imported material, destroying the pre-existing track, which [[Adam Watson (scientist)|Adam Watson]] had identified as being a 19th-century hand-made cart track.<ref>Adam Watson, ''Vehicle hill tracks in northern Scotland'', Paragon Publishing, 2011</ref> In ''Vehicle hill tracks in northern Scotland'', referring to this work, he wrote:
<blockquote>
a narrow path had been created, with unnecessary environmental impact on soils and vegetation from a new ditch excavated along the uphill side ... I said to [the NTS property manager] that the NTS was open to public criticism for damaging an old feature of historical interest ... [the track] has been buried under boulders and soil along its entire surface and verges. No works were needed, other than minor treatment to reduce erosion on slopes and washed-out sections.
</blockquote>
[[File:Mar Lodge Estate - Mountain Cyclists between Glen Dee and Glen Luibeg (28JUL10) (3).jpg|thumb|right|Mountain bikers between Glen Dee and Glen Luibeg]]
The Easter Charitable Trust's contribution towards the purchase was conditional, requiring that "NTS shall make continuous and constant efforts to dissuade, and where possible to prohibit, the use of mechanical or wheeled vehicles".<ref name="management_principles_2006">[https://archive.org/details/MarLodgeEstate_ManagementPrinciples_2006 ''Mar Lodge Estate Management Principles''], National Trust for Scotland, 2006</ref> The Trust initially considered that this stipulation also applied to bicycles, and signs were erected in various parts of the estate to state that the NTS has a policy of actively discouraging bike access, without actually stating that they were prohibited (outright prohibition would be contrary to the [[Land Reform Act (Scotland) 2003]]). In 2001 this policy was revised to allow bicycles to access "as far as [NTS] drive their Land Rovers".<ref name="tac51"/>

===Restructuring plantations===
When the National Trust for Scotland acquired Mar Lodge Estate there were many geometrical plantations across the estate, primarily planted during the ownership of the Panchauds to provide shelter for red deer, that were unnaturally-shaped with trees planted unnaturally-close. Within the minimal intervention philosophy was the gradual naturalisation of these plantations by (a) "the removal of all non-native [tree] species" and, (b) felling to open the structure and soften the edges of these plantations and, (c) the removal of the protective deer-fences around these plantations.

From 2011 the number of timber extraction operations increased rapidly. These timber operations have been branded as 'damaging' by some - in ''Ugly Deeside'',<ref>Adam Watson, ''Ugly Deeside'', Paragon Publishing, 2015</ref> writing about the timber extraction operation in the plantation near Bridge of Ey, Adam Watson writes :
<blockquote>
on 21 August 2012 I visited ... Wheel ruts were open drains, with run-off water and channels eroded down to a very hard indurated horizon. Excess water and eroded upper soil horizons continued down to and on to the public road, including pools that were yellow with silt laden water. There is little doubt that heavy rainstorms would move the silt-laden water along the public road and into the Ey Burn nearby ... The machines had turned the cultivated soils under the birchwood into mud and removed the fertile upper horizons, exposing the indurated horizon of acidic provenance. [[Podzol]]s in the pinewood had had their upper horizons removed or severely compacted, which will have destroyed them as podzol soil-types.

'''Leith Hall''' is a [[country house]] in [[Kennethmont, Scotland|Kennethmont]], [[Aberdeenshire]], Scotland. It was built in 1650, on the site of the medieval Peill Castle, and was the home of the Leith-Hay family for nearly three centuries. Since 1945 it has been run by the  [[National Trust of Scotland]] (NTS). Leith Hall is set in a {{convert|286|acre|km2|adj=on}} estate, with gardens included.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nts.org.uk/Visit/Leith-Hall/|title=Property Details for Leith Hall Garden & Estate |publisher=Nts.org.uk |access-date=2017-10-09}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aboutbritain.com/liethhallandgarden.htm |title=Leith Hall on |publisher=Aboutbritain.com |access-date=2010-03-15}}</ref>

==History==
The north wing of the house was constructed in 1650, on the site of the earlier Peill Castle, by James Leith of New Leslie (see [[Castle Croft]]). The east wing was added in 1756, and the south wing was built in 1797 by General [[Alexander Leith Hay]]. The west wing, containing the entrance front, was added in 1868 to complete the courtyard.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://canmore.org.uk/site/17673/leith-hall |title=Leith Hall |work=Canmore |publisher=Historic Environment Scotland}}</ref>

In 1745, Andrew Hay of Rannes hid at Leith Hall after the [[Battle of Culloden]] where he fought for [[Bonnie Prince Charlie]], later escaping to France.

During the [[First World War]] it became a temporary Red Cross hospital and housed over 500 patients.  In 1945 the house and grounds were presented to the NTS.

The writer [[Elizabeth Byrd]] rented 14 rooms with her second husband, Barrie Gaunt in the 1960s. In ''The Ghosts in My Life'' and ''A Strange and Seeing Time,'' Byrd describes the paranormal occurrences she and her husband experienced while living here.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Qd-TUu3IQMAC&q=byrd+leith+hall&pg=PT6|title=White Indian: 1755 The True Story of John Leith|last=Leith|first=Audie Dallas|date=2011-10-14|publisher=Xlibris Corporation|isbn=9781465376565|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Yankee Ghosts: Spine Tingling Encounters with the Phantoms of New York and New England|last=Holzer|first=Hans|publisher=Yankee Publishing, Inc.|year=1989|isbn=9780899091471}}</ref>

The gardens and grounds are open to the public all year round. After several years' closure the Hall was  re-opened by the NTS in 2013.

Leith Hall was featured on the paranormal investigation show "Most Haunted" during their third series. The episode aired on Tuesday 28 October 2003 on Living TV.<ref>https://www.imdb.com/title/tt4664366/?ref_=ttep_ep17 {{User-generated source|certain=yes|date=March 2022}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Leith Hall Gardens - geograph.org.uk - 94142.jpg|thumb|right|Leith Hall gardens]]
The house contains fine china, family portraits and tapestries and some interesting clocks. The hall is noted for its gardens, set in stages with each sheltered by a wall or hedge.<ref name="gg">{{cite web|url=http://www.gardens-guide.com/gardenpages/_0201.htm |title=Leith Hall & Gardens (Scotland)|publisher=Gardens-guide.com |date=2010-01-28 |access-date=2010-03-15}}</ref> The gardens contain flowering trees and shrubs, roses, fruit, vegetables and ornamental grasses.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britainsfinest.co.uk/gardens/gardens.cfm/searchazref/81001700LEIA |title=Leith Hall garden, Kennethmont, Huntly, Aberdeenshire - Gardens |publisher=Britainsfinest.co.uk |access-date=2010-03-15}}</ref> A little stream winds its way through the gravel paths and stone crevices and at the top of the garden, near the 18th century curved stables, is the circular "Moon Gate" leading to the old turnpike road, once the main thoroughfare to Aberdeen.<ref name="gg"/> There are also two nature trails, each about one and a half to two miles (3 km) long.<ref name="gg"/> The gardens also contain two ponds and a birdwatching site.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.information-britain.co.uk/showPlace.cfm?Place_ID=1623 |title=Leith Hall & Garden, an Attraction in Huntly, Grampian. Search for Grampian Attractions |publisher=Information-britain.co.uk |date=2005-10-16 |access-date=2010-03-15}}</ref>

== Ghostlore ==
In the context of [[ghostlore]], one notable [[ghost]] associated with this castle is believed to be that of Laird John Leith III. He was shot in the head after reacting angrily to a fellow diner who accused him of adulterating the grain sold from this hall.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Scottish ghost stories – witches, murder and folklore (Part 2) |url=https://www.nts.org.uk/stories/scottish-ghost-stories-witches-murder-and-folklore-part-2 |access-date=2023-04-24 |website=National Trust for Scotland |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Leith Hall Ghosts |url=https://aboutaberdeen.com/Leith-Hall-Ghosts |access-date=2023-04-24 |website=aboutaberdeen.com}}</ref>

The ghost of John is said to appear in great pain, with a dirty white bandage over his head and covering his eyes. He is often described as wearing dark green trousers and a shirt. In 1968, Novelist [[Elizabeth Byrd]] reported waking during the night to see John in [[highland dress]], his head covered in bloody bandages, standing at the foot of the bed.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Emma |date=2013-08-11 |title=Our intrepid reporter spends the night in Scotland's spookiest castle.. and lives to tell the tale |url=http://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/scottish-news/haunted-house-leith-hall-reveals-2151550 |access-date=2023-04-24 |website=Daily Record |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Other apparitional figures have also been sighted at this location.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-09-01 |title=Trees of grief |url=https://gothicnaturejournal.com/trees-of-grief/ |access-date=2023-04-24 |website=Gothic Nature Journal |language=en-US}}</ref>
